# Expert Question 1 (Round 1)

## Problem Understanding
Task 2017_D asks us to model the flow of passengers through a US airport
security checkpoint (ID check -> open screening line with bin-preparation ->
X-ray of belongings + millimeter-wave body scan -> bag re-collection),
identify bottlenecks, propose and model process modifications, run a
cultural-norm sensitivity analysis, and give TSA policy recommendations.
Available data: ~59 arrival records per channel (Pre-Check, regular) plus
per-station service-time samples (ID check x2 officers, MM-wave exits, X-ray
exits x2, bag round-trip times) spanning roughly 08:00-09:00 at one
checkpoint. External data give the TSA service standard (<30 min wait for 99%
of standard-lane arrivals) and the Pre-Check benchmark (<10 min for 99%), and
a 45% Pre-Check enrollment rate with 1 Pre-Check lane per 3 regular lanes.

## Current Stage
Before building anything, I am finalizing the backbone of the model. My
working interpretation of the data is: columns are cumulative timestamps of
passengers *exiting* each station, so successive differences give per-station
service times (e.g., ID-check officer 1 averages ~11 s; MM-wave gaps ~7-9 s;
X-ray gaps ~6-10 s; bag round-trip 8-50 s), and the gap between regular
arrivals (~15-30 s) vs. screening throughput reveals the bottleneck in the
bin-preparation/open-line stage and X-ray.

## Unresolved Strategic Decision
How should the core checkpoint model be formulated?

### Option A: Stochastic discrete-event simulation (DES)
Build a queueing DES (M/G/c-type) per zone: ID-check stations, open
screening lines with parallel lanes, X-ray + body-scan parallel service,
bag round-trip; calibrate service-time distributions on the data; simulate
baseline, modifications, and culture variants.
- Advantages: natural fit to heterogeneous service times and complex
  multi-zone flow; directly yields wait-time distributions and their
  variance; modifications (lane counts, staffing, bag-drop) are easy to
  represent; supports culture variants as behavioral parameters.
- Limitations: calibration on a small (~59 passenger) sample; results carry
  simulation error (mitigable with replications); "model" is partly
  computational.

### Option B: Analytical queueing network (M/G/1, M/M/c, M/M/c/c per zone,
  network approximation)
- Advantages: closed-form or near-closed-form wait-time expressions; cheap
  sensitivity analysis (culture parameters, lane counts); transparent
  bottlenecks via utilization.
- Limitations: exponential-service assumption is a poor fit to the short,
  right-skewed service times; hard to represent bag round-trips,
  bin-preparation blocking, and zone interdependencies; variance of
  end-to-end wait is only approximated.

### Option C: Hybrid — analytical M/G/c (Pollaczek-Khinchine) per station
  for bottleneck diagnosis, wrapped in DES for modification and culture
  scenarios
- Advantages: rigorous bottleneck identification (utilization +
  Pollaczek-Khinchine CV^2 terms show why variance is high) plus faithful
  scenario comparison.
- Limitations: two layers of modeling to keep consistent.

## Why This Matters
This choice fixes the structure of tasks (a)-(d), the calibration effort,
and the credibility of the throughput/variance claims in the final
submission. I recommend **Option C (hybrid, DES as the workhorse with
analytical M/G/c diagnostics)**, and ask the expert to confirm or redirect.

# Expert Question 2 (Round 2)

## Build so far (Round-1 feedback applied)
Hybrid backbone as directed: analytical M/G/c + Pollaczek-Khinchine (Erlang-C
blocking probability) as the diagnostic layer, DES as the workhorse; both fed
the same gamma (method-of-moments) service-time fits. Data reading: C/D =
ID-check service durations (~11 s per officer); E = MM-wave exit timestamps
(inter-exit ~11.6 s); F/G = two X-ray units' exit timestamps (inter-exit ~6.6 s
per unit); H = bag belt round-trip 8-50 s (mean 28.6 s). Baseline config:
6 regular + 2 Pre-Check open lines, 3+1 X-ray units, 2+1 MM-wave scanners,
2+1 ID officers; peak demand 14.8 pax/min (data arrival rates x1.5), 45%
Pre-Check.

## New strategic decision: Pre-Check lane/equipment ratio
The diagnostics expose a structural conflict that the data itself documents:
the recorded sample implies Pre-Check is ~56-58% of arrivals, and the problem
statement says ~45% enroll, while TSA opens only 1 Pre-Check lane per 3
regular lanes (~25% of capacity). In the baseline DES, Pre-Check sub-system
utilization is >1 (open lines rho=1.22, its single X-ray unit rho=3.7, single
MM-wave rho=1.29), so the Pre-Check queue is unstable and dominates end-to-end
wait variance, whereas the regular sub-system is stable (regular X-ray rho
0.55). The problem statement's own wording ("despite the fact that more
passengers use the Pre-Check process") points at this as the intended
bottleneck.

### Option A: Fix the mismatch as an explicit finding; recommend dynamic
lane sharing / demand-proportional Pre-Check allocation in the policy
recommendations, but keep the 25% allocation in the "current process"
baseline to stay faithful to the as-is system.
- Advantages: baseline honestly reproduces the reported O'Hare-style long
  lines and high variance; the modification set (M1 added capacity, M2
  pre-binning, M3 combined + dynamic Pre-Check rebalancing) has a clear
  before/after story; matches the problem's emphasis on creative solutions.
- Limitations: baseline Pre-Check sub-system is unstable (unbounded queues in
  simulation, truncated at horizon), so some reported baseline numbers are
  lower bounds.

### Option B: Rebalance Pre-Check to its demand share (45-56%) in the baseline.
- Advantages: all sub-systems stable; cleaner numbers.
- Limitations: no longer models the current process; the "bottleneck"
  disappears before we can demonstrate fixing it; conflicts with the stated
  1:3 lane rule.

### Option C: Keep baseline as-is but split all reported metrics by
  regular vs. Pre-Check, with Pre-Check truncated at horizon (documented).
- Advantages: most faithful, transparent.
- Limitations: more complex reporting.

## Why this matters
It decides what the "current process" baseline represents and how the
throughput/variance improvements from task (b) are measured. I recommend
**Option A** (baseline faithful to the 1:3 rule + instability as the headline
bottleneck finding; M3's dynamic rebalancing is the fix, and task (d)
recommends demand-proportional lane allocation as policy). Please confirm or
redirect before I finalize the scenario set and write the submission.

# Expert Question 3 (Round 3)

## Current state
Rounds 1-2 fully applied: hybrid M/G/c (diagnostic) + DES (all reported
numbers), faithful 1:3 Pre-Check baseline, stream-split reporting,
demand-proportional rebalancing as M3 centerpiece. The full scenario battery
(baseline, M1/M2/M3, demand m=1.0/1.5/2.0, Pre-Check share 45%/58%, four
culture variants, slow-traveler x M3) ran and is internally consistent:
- Baseline: Pre-Check sub-system unstable (rho = 1.2 ID, 3.6 X-ray, 1.5
  MM-wave) -> PC p99 wait 30.7 min (documented lower bound, 2 h truncation),
  total wait variance 59.4 min^2 dominated by the PC stream; regular stream
  healthy (p99 1.8 min, meets TSA <30-min-99% standard).
- M3 (rebalance to 3/10 lines, 2/5 X-ray, 2/4 MM-wave + 2nd PC ID officer +
  pre-binning): makes every PC sub-system stable (max rho 0.83); PC mean wait
  12.4 -> 0.36 min, PC p99 30.7 -> 0.74 min, total variance 59.4 -> 0.1 min^2,
  100% of travelers under 30 min. M1/M2 alone move little because the PC
  sub-system, not regular-lane capacity, is the bottleneck.
- Culture sensitivity (US +8% prep, Swiss -15%, Chinese -25% prep / -10% mm,
  slow traveler +20% prep / +15% mm): under the as-is system the styles move
  regular-lane waits by only ~10-30% (open lines rho 0.5) but do nothing for
  the PC instability; under M3 the style gap essentially closes (PC mean wait
  0.36 vs 0.39 min) — structure fixes the variance, culture only trims
  regular-lane slack.

## Final strategic decision: interpretation of the regular-lane X-ray rho
The belt side: bag round-trip (mean 28.6 s, CV 0.23, the binding constraint
per bag) vs X-ray belt scan (unit-1 inter-exit 7.5 s, unit-2 3.7 s in the
sample). If the round-trip is the per-bag service time at 3 units, regular
X-ray rho = 0.64 (stable, matches the DES); if the 12.5 s per-exit reading
for unit 1 is the service time, rho = 1.46 (unstable). The DES uses
max(scan, round-trip) per bag, so regular-lane stability hinges on this
reading. Two defensible interpretations:
- **Reading A (adopted):** column F/G are cumulative exit streams whose
  inter-exit gaps (7.5 s / 3.7 s) are belt cycle times, and the 28.6 s
  round-trip (column H, measured per passenger) is the binding per-bag
  service time (belt dwell + collection). Regular X-ray rho = 0.64, stable;
  the "output falls behind arrivals" pattern in the recorded window is
  driven by the Pre-Check share and surges, not a structurally unstable
  regular belt.
- **Reading B:** the inter-exit gaps themselves are the per-bag service
  times (unit 1 runs at 7.5 s/bag; unit 2 at 3.7 s implies a faster or
  recently repaired unit); column H is a passenger-side observation that
  partially overlaps the scan. Regular X-ray rho ~ 1.0-1.5 at peak, i.e.,
  the regular belt is ALSO near-unstable, making the as-is checkpoint
  structurally unstable on both streams and strengthening M1 (more X-ray
  units) as a necessary component.

Reading A is what the numbers and DES currently embody; Reading B would
change the baseline's regular-stream results (longer regular waits) and
elevate M1's importance. This is the last calibration judgment that can
move the headline; everything else is settled. I recommend **Reading A**
(round-trip as binding per-bag service time; cycle times reported as
throughput ceilings) and ask for confirmation or a redirect before I write
the submission container.
expert_answers:
Confirm Option C. The hybrid is the right backbone: use the analytical M/G/c layer (with Pollaczek-Khinchine CV² terms) to diagnose bottlenecks and explain variance, and the DES as the workhorse for modifications and culture scenarios. This matches the problem's dual demand for bottleneck identification and scenario comparison.

One redirect: treat the analytical layer as diagnostic, not as the source of reported wait-time distributions. Given the small samples and right-skewed service times, calibrate DES service-time distributions empirically (or via fitted lognormal/gamma), and report end-to-end wait variance only from DES replications. Keep the two layers consistent by feeding the same fitted service-time parameters into both.

Confirm Option A, with one refinement drawn from Option C: keep the 1:3 baseline faithful to the as-is system, and report all metrics split by regular vs. Pre-Check, documenting Pre-Check truncation at the horizon as a lower bound. This preserves the instability as the headline bottleneck finding while keeping the before/after story clean and honest.

Do not rebalance the baseline (reject Option B). The 1:3 rule is the documented current process, and the problem statement itself flags the mismatch, so the fix belongs in the modification set, not the baseline.

Make M3's demand-proportional Pre-Check rebalancing the centerpiece of task (b), and carry it into task (d) as the primary policy recommendation.

Confirm Reading A. The round-trip time in column H is a per-passenger measurement and is the defensible binding per-bag service time; the F/G inter-exit gaps are belt cycle times and should be reported as throughput ceilings, not as service times. This keeps the regular stream stable (rho 0.64), consistent with the DES and with the problem's framing that the Pre-Check allocation mismatch, not regular-lane capacity, is the headline bottleneck.

Do not adopt Reading B. Elevating M1 to "necessary" would dilute the M3-centered narrative that Rounds 1-2 established, and it rests on treating a cumulative exit stream as a service-time stream, which the data description does not support.

State Reading A explicitly in the submission as a calibration assumption, note Reading B as a sensitivity check on the regular belt, and keep M1 as a supporting modification rather than a required one.
